Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National International Men’s Day: Seven in 10 Ghanaian men have experienced violence in their lifetime – Gender Ministry Source : Emmanuel Tetteh 19 November 2026 7:23pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection has raised concerns about the health, mental well-being and exposure to violence among men and boys in Ghana, citing findings that about seven in 10 men have experienced at least one form of violence in their lifetime.
The Ministry said the figures highlighted the need for greater attention to men's welfare, stronger support systems and a collective effort to promote positive masculinity and build a violence-free society.
In a statement to mark International Men's Day on Wednesday, November 19, the Ministry said men continued to face significant challenges, including preventable diseases, occupational hazards, mental health difficulties and violence, many of which remained underreported.
It noted that although men were often expected to demonstrate strength and provide for their families, the pressures associated with these expectations could have serious consequences for their physical and mental well-being.
International Men's Day is observed annually on November 19 to recognise the positive contributions of men and boys, promote positive male role models and draw attention to issues affecting their health and welfare.
The Ministry said the 2026 celebration was being held under the global theme, "The Future Is Everyone" , which emphasises the importance of collective responsibility in achieving gender equality and building a fairer, healthier and safer society.
It stressed that gender equality should not be viewed as a contest between men and women but as a shared responsibility requiring the participation of everyone.
Highlighting the health challenges confronting men, the Ministry said a boy born in Ghana today could expect to live approximately 63.7 years, nearly five years less than a girl, whose life expectancy stands at about 68.6 years.
It attributed much of the disparity to late health-seeking behaviour, risky lifestyles, occupational hazards and preventable diseases.
The Ministry also expressed concern about the mental health burden among men, particularly the pressure to provide for their families and the stigma associated with financial difficulties and unemployment.
Citing studies based on World Health Organisation data, it said suicide rates among men in Ghana were higher than those among women in every year between 2000 and 2019, with older men being the most affected.
It further referenced research by the University of Ghana, which found that suicidal behaviour in the country was largely a male problem, closely linked to societal expectations for men to act as providers and the shame many experience when they lose their jobs or sources of income.
The Ministry recalled Ghana's 2023 decision to decriminalise attempted suicide, describing it as an important step towards ensuring that people experiencing psychological distress receive care rather than punishment.
It called for sustained efforts to build on the progress and encourage men to seek help when confronted with emotional and mental health difficulties.
The statement also drew attention to violence against men, citing a national study on domestic violence conducted by the Ghana Statistical Service and its partners.
According to the Ministry, the study found that approximately seven in 10 men had experienced at least one form of violence in their lifetime, while one in five had experienced domestic violence within the preceding 12 months.
It added that men reported higher levels of physical violence than women, with most of the incidents occurring outside the home.
However, the Ministry emphasised that men also had a critical responsibility to help end violence against women and girls.
Citing the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey, it said two in five women who had ever been in a relationship had experienced emotional, physical or sexual violence at the hands of a partner.
It further noted that about one in 10 men still believed that a husband was justified in beating his wife under certain circumstances.
The Ministry said the statistics demonstrated the interconnected nature of the well-being of men, women and children, warning that neglecting the welfare of men and boys had consequences for entire families and communities.
It advocated positive masculinity, characterised by care, respect and responsibility, as an important tool for tackling violence and promoting peaceful homes and communities.
As part of its recommendations, the Ministry urged men and boys to prioritise their health by undertaking regular medical check-ups and speaking openly about their challenges.
It stressed that seeking help should be regarded as a sign of strength rather than weakness.
It also encouraged men to become positive role models who reject violence at home, in workplaces and within their communities.
Families were urged to raise boys who could express their emotions, respect women and girls, and participate in household responsibilities.
The Ministry further called on families to pay greater attention to the welfare of men in their lives and regularly check on their well-being.
Traditional and religious leaders were encouraged to use their platforms to promote positive masculinity and condemn all forms of violence.
Employers were also urged to prioritise workplace health, safety and mental well-being while creating conditions that enable fathers to play active roles in their children's lives.
The Ministry called on the media and civil society organisations to highlight positive male role models and help break the silence surrounding men's physical health, mental health and experiences of violence.
The Ministry reminded survivors of violence, irrespective of their gender, that they were protected under the Domestic Violence Act, 2007 (Act 732).
It urged victims to report abuse to the Domestic Violence and Victim Support Unit (DOVVSU) of the Ghana Police Service or the nearest Department of Social Welfare office.
Looking ahead to the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, which begins on November 25, the Ministry called on men and boys across the country to participate as allies and champions in the campaign.
It encouraged Ghanaians to share messages promoting men's health, positive masculinity and violence prevention using the hashtags #InternationalMensDay, #TheFutureIsEveryone and #ViolenceFreeGhana.
The Ministry reaffirmed its appreciation for the contributions of men and boys to national development, stressing that their health, voices and examples mattered in building a peaceful society.
"Together, let us build a Ghana where every man, woman, boy and girl lives in dignity, safety and peace," it said.
